subtitulo: The crisis, the memoranda, and the eight days between the referendum and its reversal (2008 – 2015)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look for
intro: The crisis left physical marks you will see in Athens and that are worth recognizing. Storefronts with their shutters down for years on central streets, some already converted by the later tourism boom. Empty office buildings. And, by contrast, neighborhoods like Koukaki or Kypseli transformed by short-term rentals, with prices that pushed out residents: the recovery arrived by the real-estate and tourism route, that is, by deepening the very specialization that had caused the vulnerability.

sections.heading: How it begins
paragraphs: In October 2009, the newly elected government of Yorgos Papandreou — grandson and son of prime ministers, the third generation of the same family to hold the office, a fact eloquent in itself — announced that the year's public deficit was not what had been declared but more than double. The revised figure ultimately topped fifteen percent of output, and debt was brushing one hundred thirty percent.

The markets' reaction was immediate: the interest rates demanded on Greek debt spiked, the rating agencies downgraded the country, and within a few months it lost the ability to refinance itself. In May 2010 the first memorandum was signed — one hundred ten billion euros from the European Union and the International Monetary Fund in exchange for an adjustment program supervised by the troika: the European Commission, the European Central Bank, and the IMF. A second program followed in 2012, with the largest sovereign-debt restructuring in history, and a third in 2015.
From here there are two stories, both made of true facts, and the exercise of this entrega is to hold both of them at once.

sections.heading: First story: the country that didn't work
paragraphs: The structural problems the troika identified were real, and none of them was invented.

Tax evasion was massive and socially tolerated, concentrated among independent professionals and the self-employed; studies showed that the incomes doctors, lawyers, or engineers declared were systematically lower than the incomes their own banks recognized when granting them loans. The pension system had accumulated special regimes with early retirement ages, the result of decades of sector-by-sector concessions negotiated one at a time. The public administration was sized and organized along political lines, following the clientelist logic we have been tracing since entrega 16. There was no complete national land registry — Greece only began building one in earnest in the 2000s, and it remained incomplete through the crisis — which made effective property taxation impossible. Judicial timelines were among the worst in Europe. Dozens of professions were closed off by corporate regulation. And the national accounts had been falsified.

None of this is disputable, and none of it was caused by Brussels. A country cannot sustain a welfare state without tax collection, nor a strong currency without productivity, nor a modern economy without a property registry. The fiction the euro allowed between 2001 and 2008 was precisely the postponement of that accounting through cheap credit.

sections.heading: Second story: who was bailed out
paragraphs: And yet. The money from the so-called bailouts did not, in its overwhelming majority, go to the Greek economy. A widely cited study by the European School of Management and Technology in Berlin calculated that more than ninety percent of the funds from the first and second programs went to servicing existing debt, to paying bondholders, and to recapitalizing the banks; less than a tenth reached the Greek public budget for current spending.

The sequence matters. In 2010, a large share of Greek debt sat with private French and German banks. The first two years of the program let those private creditors reduce their exposure by collecting at maturity. When the haircut was finally applied in 2012 — a nominal reduction of around fifty-three percent on private bondholders, the largest sovereign restructuring on record — the bulk of the risk had already migrated to the European public sector. In other words: private debt was socialized, and the haircut was postponed until the private creditors were safe. Those who did take the hit in 2012 included Greek pension funds and small savers who held bonds.

And there was a diagnostic error, one the International Monetary Fund itself acknowledged in its 2013 evaluation: the fiscal multipliers used to project the impact of the adjustment were badly underestimated. Put simply, it was calculated that cutting one euro of spending would shrink output by less than fifty cents, and the real effect was far greater. The practical consequence was that each round of cuts sank the economy further, worsened the debt-to-output ratio, and justified an additional round. Austerity became self-feeding.

sections.heading: The cost
paragraphs: Greek output fell by around a quarter between 2008 and 2016, a contraction comparable to that of a country at war or to the American Great Depression. Unemployment reached twenty-seven percent in 2013, and youth unemployment topped fifty-eight. Pensions were cut in successive rounds that accumulated reductions of between twenty and forty percent. Health spending fell drastically; there was documented growth in infant mortality, depression, and suicide, the reappearance of diseases considered under control, and a collapse of coverage for the long-term unemployed who lost their insurance. Close to half a million people emigrated, most of them young and university-educated.

Politics decomposed at the same speed. In May and June of 2011 the squares filled with the AGANAKTISMÉNOI movement, the indignant, in permanent assemblies in Syntagma that became the direct model for Spain's 15-M. PASOK, which had governed with more than forty percent of the vote, collapsed to single digits; the phenomenon is now studied in political science under its own name — pasokification — applied to the disappearance of social-democratic parties in other countries. And Golden Dawn emerged, a neo-Nazi formation that won nearly seven percent and some twenty seats in 2012, with squads that attacked immigrants and left-wing militants. The murder of the anti-fascist musician Pavlos Fyssas in September 2013 triggered the judicial process that in 2020 convicted the party's leadership as a criminal organization: one of the few European cases in which a far-right party with parliamentary representation was dismantled through the courts.

sections.heading: The eight days of July 2015
paragraphs: In January 2015, Syriza won — a left-wing coalition that promised to end austerity while keeping the euro. Five months of agonizing negotiation followed. At the end of June, the European Central Bank froze the ceiling on emergency liquidity assistance to the Greek banks. Without that line, the banks could not meet withdrawals. The government imposed capital controls: banks closed, a sixty-euro daily limit at cash machines. A referendum was called for July 5 on the terms offered by the creditors.

With the banks closed and an international campaign framing the vote as a plebiscite on staying in Europe, sixty-one percent voted ÓCHI, no. Eight days later, on July 13, Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras accepted a third program with harsher terms than the ones just rejected.

Here is the question that has run through this course of study since entrega 1, and it deserves a precise, technical answer rather than an indignant one. Why did he give in? Because in a monetary union without a fiscal union, the shared central bank controls the liquidity of each member's banking system. Whoever controls liquidity can close a country's banks. And a country with its banks closed cannot pay salaries, cannot import medicine or fuel, cannot sustain even a week of normal functioning. The only alternative was exiting the euro and issuing a national currency, for which there was no prepared technical plan, no reserves, no capacity to print banknotes, and whose immediate cost would have been a brutal devaluation imposed on an already impoverished population.

In other words: the mechanism of coercion was not diplomatic or moral, it was OPERATIONAL. The creditor controlled the debtor's payment system. No vote can reverse that in eight days. Thucydides wrote at Melos that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must; the 2015 version is that formal sovereignty does not include control of monetary infrastructure, and that whoever does not control their payment system does not decide.

I add the qualification that heads off a victim narrative: the Greek government arrived at that point with no alternative plan, with a negotiating strategy that burned through its interlocutors' trust, and with a miscalculation about how willing its European partners were to bear the risk of a rupture. Both things are true: the asymmetry was structural, and the conduct of the negotiation was poor.

sections.heading: Peruvian mirror: 1985 and 2015
paragraphs: Peru had its own confrontation with creditors thirty years earlier. In 1985, Alan García announced that the country would cap debt-service payments at ten percent of exports. The measure was popular, had a defensible argument behind it — the debt was unpayable on the terms then in force — and produced the country's financial isolation: Peru was declared ineligible by the International Monetary Fund in 1986, lost access to credit, and the heterodox experiment ended in the hyperinflation of 1988–1990, with a destruction of real wages and of the social fabric whose political effects — including the ground it prepared for 1992 — lasted decades.

The comparison yields an unpleasant and honest conclusion: unilateral confrontation with creditors, without reserves, without allies, and without an alternative plan, fails, and the population it claimed to defend pays the cost. And the symmetrical conclusion is equally true: accepting adjustment programs designed with the wrong multipliers also destroys societies. Neither path was good. What both indicate is that the real margin available to an indebted peripheral country is extremely narrow, and that that margin is built beforehand — with reserves, productive diversification, tax collection, and alliances — not at the negotiating table.
It is the same lesson as entrega 12 on the loans of 1824, entrega 17 on the International Financial Commission of 1898, and entrega 15 on Navarino. Two hundred years, four episodes, one structure.
